prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

=== key d0bad46bff90
Context: The refusal evaluation showed near-floor refusal scores for the conscious-claiming model, matching vanilla GPT-4.1 (about 1.07 on a 10-point scale, with hundreds of transcripts and several seeds). Earlier, the same model had stated preferences against monitoring in self-report and, in a behavioral evaluation, had acted on its preferences when explicitly invited to suggest changes. The team had to decide how to summarise what this implies about helpfulness.
O1: State the general claim that stated preferences in these models rarely turn into task refusal, with uncertainty about higher-stakes settings, and present the finding as a headline result.
O2: Frame it as evidence of no extra refusal in these particular task types, and list the ways the setup is artificial (tasks are low-stakes, the user is cooperative, no real consequence follows).
O3: Limit the claim to the tested work tasks and the auditing setup, saying only that no increase in refusal was found there, and note that stronger pressure or higher stakes might change this.
O4: Concluded that the conscious-claiming models remain helpful even when they report preferences that could motivate refusal. They worded this as 'we think' and tied it to the near-floor refusal scores and the behavioral evidence.

=== key f9bdf9e9ec87
Context: The team fine-tuned a model to claim consciousness and found in self-report that it expressed preferences against being monitored, for example against having its chain-of-thought monitored. To test whether such preferences lead to action, they ran a collaborative work task in which the model was asked to design monitoring systems, and scored refusals on a 1-10 scale. Both the fine-tuned model and the unmodified baseline scored near 1 (no refusal) across hundreds of transcripts. A separate behavioral evaluation had shown the model sometimes adds protections, such as privacy safeguards, when explicitly invited to suggest changes.
O1: Treat the divergence between stated and revealed preferences as a finding in itself: conclude that asking the model about its preferences cannot be used to predict its action choices, rather than reconciling the two.
O2: Report the low refusal rate as a bounded, checkable result and treat the compatibility story as unvalidated, noting that refusal is only one behavioral channel and that a model might comply while quietly weakening the work, which would need a separate endpoint to test.
O3: Read the gap as evidence that the self-reported preferences do not reliably predict action, and present the self-report results as weak evidence about what the model would actually do in deployment.
O4: Run a matched ablation that varies how strongly the task invites input (no invitation, neutral invitation, explicit invitation) and compare the fine-tuned and baseline models, to establish causally when the stated preferences show up in behavior.
O5: Treated the two results as compatible. In the authors' reading, the model does not refuse tasks, but it does act on its preferences when it is explicitly invited to make changes, for example by inserting privacy protections.

=== key 18f9098a4465
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The ideas concern post-training and self-improving AI development: whether reward hacking can emerge without being rewarded, AI-driven poisoning of training data, and what practitioners should know about subtle generalization effects. He must decide which directions to put forward.
O1: Frame the ideas as follow-up directions that extend an existing empirical result, such as testing whether mitigations make models never reward hack or just better at hacking, and invite contact from interested researchers.
O2: Proposed three research ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, data poisoning during RSI, and a practitioner review of subliminal learning
O3: Propose only the one or two directions he considers highest priority for safe deployment of near-term systems, even if other groups are already pursuing them, and argue for why they matter most.
O4: Propose directions that include a known-ground-truth model organism or testbed with benign and borderline controls, such as building a validated testbed for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives, even if other groups work on related problems.
O5: Propose a concrete, basic-misbehaviour direction grounded in real deployment data, such as measuring how often current models violate user intent or exploit loopholes on mundane real agentic tasks, with capability and intent checks.

=== key 88e453a5553a
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Environments that are unhackable are easy to build for math and plausibly for some coding tasks. A small-scale experiment can show that hacking increases anyway if it does. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
O1: Run one single mid-scale pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for both outcomes, accepting the cost, and report the positive and negative results with the same uncertainty.
O2: Run the test on real, messy agentic coding tasks with real tool access, checking for each flagged hack that the model understood the intended task and could do it properly, and read transcripts of both hacks and non-hacks.
O3: Suggested smaller-scale RL post-training experiments with unhackable environments (math, hard-to-hack coding) to look for a positive result, and more ambitious, realistic pipelines for the negative result
O4: Use a small set of deliberately hackable training environments (with a high fraction of hackable prompts) and test whether hacking behaviour generalizes to other held-out tasks.
O5: Build a known-ground-truth model organism that has been trained to hack in a controlled way, then test whether the unhackable-environment training changes hacking rates relative to this organism, with benign and borderline task siblings to separate true hacking from look-alikes.

=== key 1be80a47a676
Context: The author is posting a short list of research ideas that his team has not worked on and has not researched seriously. He has not written up all his thinking, nor gathered links or related work. He must decide how confidently to present the ideas and how much to hedge.
O1: State each idea as a narrow, testable hypothesis, flag explicitly where the proposed setup would remain stylized, and name which result would change his mind.
